name: Nobotara Apollo 11 Offline Voiceovers
description: Pre-rendered offline audio voiceover clips for Apollo 11 and Voyager 1

clips.speaker: Neil Armstrong
clips.text: Hey, Neil Armstrong here. On July 16, 1969, we rode a Saturn V built from math, sweat, and nerve. 384,000 km to test physics where mistakes could kill. We didn’t just chase a rock in the sky; we went to learn what people can do when they dare.

clips.speaker: Neil Armstrong
clips.text: This is the Eagle’s descent stage. It helped the Lunar Module land on the Moon. The ascent stage carried me and Aldrin back into lunar orbit, while the descent stage remained behind.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: The Lunar Module was built in two distinct stages. The descent stage contained the throttleable rocket engine, landing gear, and propellant tanks. Since weight was critical for orbital rendezvous, only the lightweight ascent stage lifted off to return to Earth.

clips.speaker: Neil Armstrong
clips.text: Not everything left behind became inactive. Apollo 11 astronauts placed this laser retroreflector. Scientists on Earth can send laser pulses toward it and measure the returning light to study the distance between Earth and the Moon.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: Observatories in Texas, Hawaii, and France still bounce high-energy pulsed lasers off this Apollo 11 reflector. By timing the ~2.5 second round-trip with picosecond accuracy, scientists proved the Moon is drifting away at 3.8 cm per year.

clips.speaker: Neil Armstrong
clips.text: This plaque commemorates humanity’s first crewed lunar landing. It carries a message of peace from Earth. A message left behind for history to remember.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: Engraved on stainless steel to withstand cosmic radiation and 300°C temperature swings: 'HERE MEN FROM THE PLANET EARTH FIRST SET FOOT UPON THE MOON JULY 1969 A.D. WE CAME IN PEACE FOR ALL MANKIND.'

clips.speaker: Neil Armstrong
clips.text: Good work, explorer. You understand why we left these pieces behind: for science, for survival, and for peace. The lunar surface keeps our story safe.

clips.speaker: Neil Armstrong
clips.text: The footprints at Tranquility Base proved that humanity could leave Earth. But our journey didn't stop at the Moon. We aimed further—beyond the planets, into interstellar space.

clips.speaker: Narrator-02
clips.text: Humanity once stood on the Moon, leaving behind the marks of its first steps. But exploration was never meant to end there. Beyond the Moon, beyond Mars, beyond the familiar boundaries of our Solar System, another journey continued. A machine built on Earth, launched in 1977, sent to explore the outer planets. It travelled farther than any human-made spacecraft before it. In August 2012, Voyager 1 entered interstellar space. It had crossed a boundary humanity had never crossed before.

clips.speaker: Mission Control
clips.text: Voyager 1, your signal is faint, but we are listening. You have travelled farther than we ever imagined. Turn the spacecraft until the high-gain antenna points at Earth.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: Voyager uses a high-gain antenna fixed to the body of the spacecraft. The whole craft has to turn so that dish faces Earth. That link is how its instruments send scientific data home. At this distance a radio message takes many hours to arrive.

clips.speaker: Narrator-02
clips.text: The Sun's influence reaches far beyond the planets. But there is a frontier where its protective bubble gives way to the interstellar environment. Voyager 1 crossed that frontier in August 2012. Now it is exploring a region no human-made spacecraft had entered before.

clips.speaker: Narrator-02
clips.text: The first reading is a plasma wave. Out here the instrument listens to the thin electrical tremble of the gas around the spacecraft.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: Plasma-wave measurements can reveal properties of the surrounding environment. What you see is an educational reading of an instrument Voyager really carries. The game is not performing a new scan.

clips.speaker: Narrator-02
clips.text: The next reading is the magnetic field. Scientists compare its strength and direction with what the heliosphere would produce.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: Magnetic-field measurements help scientists tell the solar bubble from the interstellar medium beyond it. This panel is an interpretation of that investigation, not a fresh measurement made for the game.

clips.speaker: Narrator-02
clips.text: The third reading counts charged particles. Their numbers change as the spacecraft leaves the Sun's wind behind.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: Particle measurements help scientists investigate the space beyond the heliosphere. The display explains that capability. It does not claim Voyager is taking a new sample right now.

clips.speaker: Narrator-02
clips.text: Every mission has limits. Voyager was never designed to operate forever. Its power supply slowly weakens, and engineers must decide which systems can continue and which must be switched off. Sometimes, keeping a mission alive means learning to do less.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: NASA has made real decisions to switch off Voyager instruments to conserve power. This is a long-term engineering trade-off, not a sudden failure of the spacecraft.

clips.speaker: Narrator-02
clips.text: Voyager carries something more than instruments. The Golden Record holds sounds from our world: wind, surf, animals, and tools.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: The Golden Record is real. Its sound essay was chosen to represent Earth. The record is not a device that transmits those sounds back to Earth.

clips.speaker: Narrator-02
clips.text: It also carries greetings in human languages. A civilisation wanted to say, across every barrier of speech: we were here.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: The greetings were recorded in dozens of languages. They are a message to whoever might one day find the spacecraft. They are not a live broadcast.

clips.speaker: Narrator-02
clips.text: The record also stores images: people, animals, the planet, and how we build. Scientists and collaborators chose them to represent life on Earth.

clips.speaker: Scientific Voice
clips.text: The images were encoded on the disc with music and the sounds. The record rides with Voyager. It does not send its contents home.
